item.text: {"question_id":"5B.10","answer":"The evidence does not establish that López Obrador left a clearly stronger, fairer, and durable economic trajectory than he inherited. There were material gains during the period: 2023 GDP grew about 3.2–3.3%, employment and real labor income increased, labor poverty declined, inflation fell, macroeconomic stability was preserved, and the administration expanded pensions and social transfers and negotiated USMCA continuity (BATCH-0052-E019; BATCH-0049-E004; BATCH-0054-E002; BATCH-0032-E006; BATCH-0016-E013). These outcomes cannot be attributed wholly to the ruler: recovery reflected the pandemic rebound, U.S. recovery and demand, nearshoring, foreign investment, remittances, terms of trade, and autonomous monetary institutions (BATCH-0052-E014; BATCH-0052-E019; BATCH-0054-E002). Against them, GDP and GDP per capita remained below 2018 levels in the latest comparable data; potential growth remained subdued because of low productivity and limited investment; informality, regional and income disparities, and regulatory and infrastructure constraints persisted (BATCH-0032-E001; BATCH-0022-R02-E001; BATCH-0052-E014). Distributional and household evidence was mixed: multidimensional poverty fell, but extreme poverty was broadly unchanged or higher in absolute terms, social deprivation increased for some groups, and health-service deprivation worsened sharply, especially among lower-income people (BATCH-0032-E002; BATCH-0032-E003; BATCH-0054-E002). Durability and implementation are also unresolved. Only eight of 24 World Bank objective indicators were achieved, while ten were off track; projects were cancelled, restructured, delayed, or narrowed amid changing priorities and institutional-capacity constraints (BATCH-0052-E014; BATCH-0052-E015; BATCH-0052-E020). Flagship investment and PEMEX support therefore produced substantial sustainability concerns, including weak PEMEX finances, incomplete projects, possible medium-term crowd-out of education and infrastructure, and unresolved Tren Maya documentation and transfer problems (BATCH-0052-E019; BATCH-0014-E014; BATCH-0040-E008). The best-supported conclusion is a mixed end-period trajectory: attributable social and labor-policy gains and macroeconomic resilience coexisted with weak productivity, incomplete implementation, worsening service access, uneven distribution, and insufficient evidence that the gains were durable beyond the recovery
